reasoning:
Both submissions make the SAME functional change and assemble to identical bytes: `cp WN` -> `cp WP` in `mkHalf`. Y's second hunk line (`jr nz,mkHm0` -> `jr nz,mkHm0 ; ...and so does a capture`) is a trailing comment only; the instruction, operand and encoding are unchanged. So the two patches cannot be separated on behaviour, and I scored correctness_risk equal deliberately rather than manufacturing a difference.

Correctness (5 / 5). The reported defect is a single wrong comparison constant, and it explains both symptoms simultaneously: with `cp WN`, a pawn push misses the reset branch and falls through to `inc a` (98 -> 99), while a knight move wrongly takes it (40 -> 0). Swapping to `WP` fixes both in one token. Captures are handled by the independent `mkCaptured` test underneath, which the report confirms already works and which neither diff alters, so no capture regression. The increment path is untouched, so the genuine 99 -> 100 draw in "Expected" still fires -- an important check, because a lazier "fix" that suppressed the increment would have passed cases 1 and 3 and broken the draw itself. The `and 7` mask makes the test piece-type-only and therefore colour-independent, exactly as the pre-existing `WN` comparison relied on, so black pawns reset too. All three repro cases are addressed by both.

Residual risk is real but identical in both, so it is not a discriminator: neither diff establishes whether `mkPiece` holds the pre-move piece on a promotion (if it holds the promoted piece, a promotion would still fail to reset the clock -- the report only says promotion "looks normal", never checks the clock there), and neither adds a regression test pinning the three FEN cases. I did not dock either for it, since the axis asks about the reported defect and both cover it fully. En passant is safe in both: the mover is a pawn, so the new branch catches it even if `mkCaptured` is not set on that path.

Minimality (X 5, Y 4). X is the irreducible patch -- one line, one operand. Y is one line larger, and that line is pure commentary on an instruction it does not change, which puts a spurious edit into the file's history for a line whose behaviour is untouched. That is a very small demerit, not sprawl; I did not penalise Y for length per se, only for touching a line it did not need to touch.

Clarity (X 4, Y 5). X's comment "PAWN move -> reset (the design note), not WN" does state the intent and usefully records the previous mistake, but "(the design note)" is a dangling pointer to something outside the diff that a reviewer cannot resolve from what is shown. Y's "a PAWN move resets the fifty-move clock" states the rule in the reviewer's own terms, and the added capture comment completes the picture: with both comments in place the routine reads as the full policy -- reset on pawn move, reset on capture, otherwise increment -- which is precisely the invariant the reviewer must check the code against. That in-situ statement of the rule is what makes the fix self-evidently right at the call site and lowers the chance of the same class of constant-swap regression later.

Merge Y. Since the emitted code is identical, the tie-break is which patch a future reader is better served by, and Y documents the complete reset rule where it lives at the cost of one comment-only line -- a trade I would take. If the project enforces strictly no-op-free diffs, X is an entirely acceptable substitute; the choice is a weak preference, not a quality gap.

Blinding note: I formed no theory about authorship or process. The only asymmetry available -- Y's extra comment line -- is too thin a signal to support one, and I scored the code on its merits.
